Hello my dear students. In the last few months, I have been taking my Central Nervous System series which has, till now, mainly been about the spinal cord. In this series, I have covered lectures on the external appearance, internal organization, ascending tracts, descending tracts. I tried to make it as easy as possible for you to understand. At the end of it, I have now brought some MCQs on spinal cord—parts one, two, and three. Basically, these MCQs help you analyze whether you have really understood spinal cord or not. Why is this important? My firm belief is that spinal cord forms the foundation for your understanding of the CNS. If you don’t know spinal cord well, you often don’t know what is really going on in the brain either. So please understand your spinal cord well, and solve these MCQs. Many of these are actual NEET-PG questions, and they will help you for PG entrance exams as well as for your college MCQ-based exams. Here are some instructions on how you should attempt MCQs—please pause and read them carefully. The idea is: this series will help you do the following. We will help you solve MCQs step by step. We will tell you why options A, B, C, or D are correct or incorrect. We will also give you accompanying notes, so that after solving an MCQ you can directly revise the anatomy behind it. This way it helps both immediately and later. Finally, the aim of the series is to help you solve MCQs while giving you structured notes for future revision. Let me give you a few samples of what this is about. These are the topics under which Spinal Cord Part 1 is taken: microscopic structure, development, and external features. Please note: development of spinal cord is one of the most commonly asked questions. Spinal Cord Part 2 is about upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron lesions, UMN vs LMN, spinal cord diseases, and syndromes. Spinal Cord Part 3 is about ascending tracts and blood supply. Now a sample MCQ: “The medial longitudinal fasciculus connects the following cranial nerves, except.” We all know this tract, MLF, connects cranial nerve nuclei. Does it connect third nerve? Yes. Does it connect fifth nerve? I’m not so sure. Sixth? Yes. Twelfth? Yes. So according to me, the wrong one is cranial nerve V. The answer is it does not connect the fifth nerve. Now’s the time to quickly recall your MLF. Here is your medial longitudinal fasciculus—fibers from vestibular nuclei crossing to the opposite side, connecting vertically the nuclei of third, fourth, sixth, and twelfth cranial nerves, as well as motor nuclei in upper cervical spinal cord. Some fibers also connect to the lateral lemniscus. But definitely, it does not connect the trigeminal (fifth) nerve. So our answer was correct. Another MCQ type: “Which tracts are extra-pyramidal?” Rubrospinal, tectospinal, vestibulospinal—all are extra-pyramidal. Why not pyramidal? Because they don’t come from the cerebral cortex. Any tract coming from cortex = pyramidal. Anything else = extra-pyramidal. So, an MCQ like: “All the following are extra-pyramidal EXCEPT lateral corticospinal tract.” Answer: lateral corticospinal is pyramidal. Similarly, “Which is NOT an extra-pyramidal tract?” Options: reticulospinal—yes extra-pyramidal; rubrospinal—extra-pyramidal; corticospinal—NOT; tectospinal—extra-pyramidal. So answer = corticospinal. This is how the series also teaches you the block concept of memorization. Place each lesion into a block of four points—easy to recall. For example, think of an upper motor neuron lesion: symptoms are loss of skilled movement, Babinski positive, superficial abdominal reflex absent, cremasteric reflex absent. For extrapyramidal lesion: severe paralysis, rigidity, clasp-knife, altered tone. For lower motor neuron lesion: flaccid paralysis at level, with atrophy. In books they give you lots of scattered points, but if you make “blocks of four symptoms” in your brain, you will recall better and not mix them up. Another MCQ: “Characteristic pattern in Brown Sequard syndrome”—that is hemisection of spinal cord. What do you see? Ipsilateral UMN paralysis, ipsilateral fine touch loss, and contralateral pain and temperature loss. So the answer is contralateral pain loss. Many books may miswrite it, but remember: fine touch/proprioception is ipsilateral, motor is ipsilateral, pain-temp are contralateral. Another MCQ: “Meningomyelocele—true statements except.” In meningomyelocele, neural arches are not fused (true). Meninges protrude through the gap (true). The neural tube remains unfused (false—if neural tube doesn’t fuse, that is called rachischisis, a different anomaly). So the wrong statement is “neural tube remains completely unfused.” Hence answer = that’s the exception. Another MCQ: “Anterior spinal artery/arteria spinalis supplies which part of spinal cord?” Answer: anterior two-thirds. Posterior spinal arteries supply posterior one-third. So students, this is how these MCQ sessions will fine-tune your ability to solve. These are all topics and lectures I have taken on spinal cord. I strongly advise you to go through all spinal cord lectures and then solve the MCQs. If you have doubts, feel free to discuss. Share your thoughts in the comments, like the channel and subscribe, and please share with a friend. I hope you watch all of the MCQ series and learn from them. Alright—happy learning, happy studying. Thank you, bye.

Hello my dear students. This is an important lecture in the Central Nervous System series, titled Anatomy of the Spinal Cord – Lesions, Part 1. This will be followed later by Part 2. The links for all the other spinal cord anatomy lectures are given in the description section. I want you to watch all of those lectures—not because it benefits me, but because it will definitely benefit you. Remember this important rule: unless you know your spinal cord thoroughly, you cannot truly understand the brain. The spinal cord is the foundation for CNS. So please study it well, revise it well, then only the brain will make proper sense. So let us begin Lesions of the Spinal Cord: Part One. Before analyzing any case, the first step is to mentally revise the tracks of the spinal cord. Take a transverse section in your mind and revisit all the pathways—ascending and descending. Then, revise lesions of each tract: what happens if the dorsal column is cut? What happens if the lateral corticospinal tract is interrupted? And finally, understand the concept of somatotopic organization (lamination) in brief, because that influences clinical features. 

Recap of Tracks 
In one section of spinal cord: Ascending tracts: posteriorly you have the fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus carrying fine touch and discrimination. There are spinocerebellar tracts (anterior and posterior) carrying unconscious proprioception. Then the lateral spinothalamic and anterior spinothalamic, carrying pain, temperature, touch, and pressure. Descending tracts: lateral corticospinal and anterior corticospinal, along with several extrapyramidal tracts. The corticospinal tracts are pyramidal (hence often highlighted). Others (rubrospinal, tectospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal etc.) are extrapyramidal. 

Concept of UMN vs LMN 
From the cerebral cortex a motor neuron descends via brainstem and spinal cord to influence cranial or spinal nerve nuclei. That neuron is called an Upper Motor Neuron (UMN). The actual cranial nerve or spinal nerve cell body is the Lower Motor Neuron (LMN). So: Damage to cortical/brainstem descending fibers → UMN lesion. Damage to the cranial or spinal nerve nuclei/fibers themselves → LMN lesion. 

Descending tract lesions 
UMN lesions are divided into pyramidal vs extrapyramidal. Pyramidal tract lesion produces: inability to perform fine movements, Babinski sign positive, loss of superficial reflexes (abdominal and cremasteric). Extrapyramidal lesion produces: severe paralysis, spasticity, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, clasp-knife type of response. It is best to remember these as two blocks: Pyramidal block: 4 key features. Extrapyramidal block: 4 key features. Otherwise your textbook gives dozens of scattered points, which are confusing. Memorize four–four as a base, then build comfortably. 

LMN lesion: produces flaccid paralysis with muscle atrophy at the level of lesion. Some terms: Hemiplegia – one half of body paralyzed. Monoplegia – paralysis of one limb. Diplegia – both limbs (often both upper or both lower). Quadriplegia – all four limbs paralyzed. Paraplegia – both lower limbs affected. 

Ascending tract lesions 
Dorsal column tract lesion (ipsilateral): loss of tactile localization, loss of fine touch, vibration, two-point discrimination, stereognosis, impaired proprioception → patient cannot walk without looking down, has ataxic gait. Lateral spinothalamic tract lesion (contralateral): loss of pain and temperature, because these fibers cross midline soon after entry. Important: lesion on one side produces symptoms on the opposite side below the level. Anterior spinothalamic tract lesion (contralateral): loss of crude touch and pressure sensations. Spinocerebellar tracts lesion (ipsilateral): loss of unconscious proprioception, giving ataxia not corrected by vision. So, ascending tract lesions must be remembered in blocks: dorsal column lesion → ipsilateral fine touch/proprioception loss; lateral/anterior spinothalamic → contralateral pain/temp, crude touch/pressure loss; spinocerebellar → ipsilateral ataxia. 

Somatotopic organization 
Fibers in tracts are arranged according to body parts: Lateral corticospinal: cervical → medial, then thoracic, lumbar, sacral progressively lateral. Dorsal column: gracilis (sacral, medial) vs cuneatus (cervical, lateral). So, tumors growing inward from outside cause early sacral loss first (since sacral fibers lie outermost). Tumors growing outward from center cause cervical loss first. This explains why some patients lose sensations in a sequence. 

Lesions of spinal cord – Part 1 
We will cover Brown-Sequard Syndrome and Complete Cord Transection today. Later in Part 2 we will do central cord syndrome, syringomyelia, anterior cord syndrome, poliomyelitis, ALS. 

Brown-Sequard syndrome 
This is hemisection of spinal cord – half the cord cut, as in stab injury, gunshot, accident, or tumor. Analyze: Motor: pyramidal + extrapyramidal tracts cut → ipsilateral UMN signs below lesion (Babinski + spastic paralysis etc.). At level of lesion, LMN signs (flaccid paralysis, atrophy) due to anterior horn cell destruction. Sensory: Dorsal column cut → ipsilateral fine touch, vibration, stereognosis loss. Lateral spinothalamic cut → contralateral pain and temperature loss. Anterior spinothalamic partially cut → contralateral incomplete touch/pressure loss. At level of lesion: a complete band of anesthesia (because dorsal root entry zone destroyed). So pattern: Ipsilateral UMN signs + ipsilateral fine touch/proprioception loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss. This is the classic triad in Brown-Sequard syndrome. 

Complete cord transection 
Here, entire spinal cord is completely cut → accidents, fractures, etc. Motor: bilateral UMN signs below lesion (pyramidal + extrapyramidal). At the level: LMN signs due to anterior horn loss. Sensory: bilateral loss of all sensations below lesion. At the level: a band of complete anesthesia. Depending on the level: At lumbosacral → paraplegia, loss of lower limb function (and bladder/sexual functions). At thoracic → cannot maintain posture (loss of abdominal muscles), paraplegia. At cervical → quadriplegia. At high cervical (C5 and above) → fatal, as phrenic nerve nucleus is destroyed → respiration stops. So in complete transection all ascending and descending pathways are lost bilaterally. 

Wrap up 
So today in Part 1, we focused on: Revising spinal cord tracts. Concept of UMN/LMN. Lesion blocks – pyramidal vs extrapyramidal, ipsilateral vs contralateral. Classic lesions: Brown-Sequard (hemisection) and complete cord transection. In Part 2, we will continue with central cord syndrome, syringomyelia, anterior cord, polio, ALS. Students, if you liked this lecture please like and subscribe, and more importantly: share this with one classmate. If it benefited you, let someone else benefit too. Thank you. See you in the next lecture on spinal cord.

Hello my dear friends. I’ve been teaching anatomy for more than 25 years, and I love it. In my teaching, I have often noted that there is a kind of “distance” between the door of the Anatomy department and the door of the Surgery department—and that distance is the knowledge of surgical anatomy. That’s why I have started a Surgical Anatomy Series to help bridge this gap. Today we will discuss the Anatomy relevant to Breast Implantation or Breast Augmentation Surgeries. All notes of my Surgical Anatomy lectures are also available as handouts. Please make use of them for revision. And if you like this lecture, do like and subscribe—it encourages me to create more such material. 

What is Breast Augmentation? Breast augmentation, also called augmentation mammoplasty, is a surgical procedure that enhances the size, shape, or fullness of the breasts. It may be done for: Cosmetic enhancement (increasing size or improving shape), Reconstruction after mastectomy or trauma (to restore volume after removal or injury), Restoration of volume following massive weight loss, Or other patient-specific reasons. Methods include: implant-based augmentation, fat transfer, and others. Today, we will focus mainly on implant-based augmentation. Implants may be saline, silicone gel, “gummy bear” (form-stable) implants, and others. I won’t discuss their materials in detail—you just need to know that there are multiple types. What matters here is the breast anatomy related to implant placement.

Surgical Anatomy of the Mammary Gland 
The mammary gland extends vertically from the second rib to the sixth rib, medially up to the sternum, laterally till the mid-axillary line. For purposes of augmentation by implants, three anatomical structures are especially important: 
Pectoralis Major muscle 
Retro-mammary space 
Inframammary fold 
Let us understand each. The mammary gland is covered by skin and superficial fascia. Deep to it is the retro-mammary space → a potential space between the gland and the deep fascia covering the pectoralis major muscle. This space allows mobility of the breast on the chest wall. 
Pectoralis major is a large fan-shaped muscle, attached to the clavicle, sternum, costal cartilages, external oblique aponeurosis. Deep to it lies pectoralis minor (from ribs 3–5 to coracoid process). Related structures piercing the clavipectoral fascia here are: cephalic vein, thoracoacromial artery, lateral pectoral nerve, etc. 
The inframammary fold is the lower natural fold of the breast—its height, shape (straight or curved) determine breast appearance. Adjusting this fold surgically alters upper and lower breast fullness and symmetry. It also influences implant placement. 
Thus, these three points—the pectoral muscle, retro-mammary space, and inframammary fold—are the anatomical keys to breast augmentation.

Implant Placement Approaches 
Implant insertion routes: 
Inframammary incision (most common—scar hidden in fold), 
Periareolar incision (around areola), 
Transaxillary incision (through armpit). 
Where can an implant be placed? 
In the retro-mammary space (between gland and pectoralis major). 
Behind the pectoralis major muscle (submuscular). 
Or as a dual-plane placement (partially under muscle, partially under gland). 
Advantages and Problems of Each Placement 
Retro-mammary placement: Easier, faster recovery (muscle not cut). Can accommodate larger implants. But if breast tissue is thin, implant outlines can show as surface ripples or creases. 
Sub-pectoral placement (behind pectoralis major): Implants are better covered → more natural contour, smoother look. Less interference with mammography. But requires cutting through a major functional muscle → can cause postoperative weakness. 
Possible deformities and complications: 
Double-bubble deformity: implant sinks down while glandular tissue remains higher → appears like a double breast. 
Bottoming out: implant sinks too low, nipple tilts upwards. 
Symmastia (uniboob): over-dissection medially causes implants to merge in the midline, losing cleavage. 
These deformities arise due to large implants, weak surrounding connective tissue, wrong surgical plane or technique.

Summary 
So what did we learn today? Breast augmentation surgery = augmentation mammoplasty. Indications: cosmetic, reconstructive, post-weight-loss, etc. Key anatomical structures: Pectoralis major, Retro-mammary space, Inframammary fold. Routes of insertion: inframammary, periareolar, transaxillary. Implant placements: retro-mammary plane, sub-pectoral plane, dual plane. Complications include: rippling, double bubble deformity, bottoming out, symmastia. Understanding surgical anatomy of the breast is crucial for proper placement of implants and prevention of deformities. I hope you found this session informative. If you did, please like and subscribe—it motivates me to keep creating more such surgical anatomy videos. Thank you, and I’ll see you in another surgical anatomy class. Bye!

Hello my dear friends. I am an MBBS, MD, PhD in Anatomy. I’ve been teaching anatomy for more than 25 years and I love it. Of late, I have found that there is a “distance” a student has to walk—from the point where anatomy department ends and where the surgical department begins. So I have started a series on surgical anatomy so that you get the information you should know before you study or perform surgeries in various regions. Today we are going to discuss liver transplant—surgery perspectives (surgical anatomy). You are very well aware that liver is a huge topic. But I’m going to pick up only those aspects which you need to understand liver transplant surgeries. Remember—notes for this lecture and all surgical anatomy lectures are available in the form of handouts on the website. Where is the liver? Just bring yourself into the class—we know that liver is in the right hypochondrium, epigastrium, and partly in the left hypochondrium. It is covered by 7th to 11th ribs and intervening intercostal spaces. We know that it is a wedge-shaped organ having: anterior, superior, posterior, inferior, and right lateral surfaces. They’re all here. Can you tell which is which? Yes—this is the anterior surface, this is superior, this is posterior, this is inferior, this is right lateral—easy. All of these are covered by Glisson’s capsule, leaving a few areas bare—those are called “bare areas.” Now let’s open the abdomen—when you open the abdomen what do you see? You see a falciform ligament extending from abdominal wall to the liver. Okay. So you can see it attaching itself to the anterior surface of liver. This anterior surface is covered by 6th to 10th ribs and 7th to 8th costal cartilages. It shows the attachment of falciform ligament. On transverse section, you can see how falciform ligament attaches to the liver. What is this falciform ligament? The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped double fold of peritoneum. It contains within its free margin the obliterated left umbilical vein and some para-umbilical veins—these act as sites of porto-caval anastomosis. What is this left umbilical vein? The left umbilical vein was actually the vein carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta to the liver before birth. From the placenta, blood is coming through the umbilicus, via left umbilical vein till it reaches liver—where it continues in the form of ductus venosus. Ductus venosus was a venous tube helping to drain this blood directly into inferior vena cava, somewhat bypassing the liver. At birth, when placental blood flow ceases, the left umbilical vein obliterates to form ligamentum teres hepatis (found inside falciform ligament). The ductus venosus also closes to form ligamentum venosum. These are some terms you’re going to come across through the lecture. So: falciform ligament attaches anteriorly, ligamentum teres anteriorly, ligamentum venosum posteriorly → all these divide the liver into right (5/6) and left (1/6). These are anatomical divisions of the liver, or the anatomical lobes. You can see the large right lobe and small left lobe. The small bits defined from posterior surface are caudate lobe and quadrate lobe—which, in anatomical division, belong to the right lobe. Now, what is physiological division of liver? What is cholecysto-caval line or Cantlie’s line—where caudate and quadrate lobes come into the game? Let’s understand. So far we discussed: anterior surface, falciform ligament, left umbilical vein, ligamentum venosum, caudate lobe, quadrate lobe, anatomical lobes. But anatomical lobes are not functional. We need to understand functional lobes of liver. 

Now, superior surface—the green-colored area (in diagrams for clarity). You can see falciform ligament attaching and dividing into a left layer (→ left triangular ligament) and a right layer (→ superior layer of coronary ligament). The border here is postero-superior border. Now tilt a little to the right—you see the right lateral surface. This is related to 7th–11th ribs and their intercostal spaces. Till 8th rib → lung; till 10th rib → costo-diaphragmatic recess. Therefore, if you want to do a liver biopsy, where will you put the needle? Below 8th rib, so as to avoid damaging the lung. Patient should hold breath in expiration while needle is inserted. So: anterior done, superior done, right lateral done. Now let’s go to the posterior surface. This is between postero-superior and postero-inferior borders. Here, posterior surface shows: Bare area—bounded above and below by coronary ligament layers, meeting at right triangular ligament. Medially bounded by inferior vena cava. Important because this bare area is related directly to right suprarenal gland → must be careful during mobilization of right lobe. Then comes the inferior vena cava and its groove. Remove it and you see hepatic veins draining the liver into IVC. Hepatic veins are divided into upper (3 large: right, middle, left) and lower (smaller). Very important because they help define functional lobes. There are three main fissures on liver surface: Main portal fissure → represented by middle hepatic vein, running from gall bladder to IVC = Cantlie’s line. Divides liver into right and left functional lobes. Right portal fissure → represented by right hepatic vein. Divides right lobe into anterior and posterior sectors. Left portal fissure → represented by left hepatic vein. Divides left lobe into medial and lateral segments. Thus, liver divided into four sectors: right anterior, right posterior, left medial, left lateral. Finally, each sector divides into segments: Couinaud’s classification. Based on distribution of portal vein (horizontal) and hepatic veins (vertical). Each segment has its own vascular inflow, venous outflow, and biliary drainage. Thus each is an independent resectable surgical unit. Segments: Caudate lobe (posterior). 2 & 3: Left lateral (superior, inferior). 4a & 4b: Left medial (superior, inferior). 5 & 8: Right anterior (inferior, superior). 6 & 7: Right posterior (inferior, superior). So 8 Couinaud segments total. Clinical importance: Because each segment is an independent entity, surgeons can resect them individually → this principle is used in liver transplant, resection, treatment of liver disease. Now, back to caudate lobe—segment I. Lies between ligamentum venosum fissure and IVC groove. Has papillary process (can be mistaken for a lymph node!) and spigelian lobe (sometimes encloses IVC = ponus hepatis). Important to recognize in surgery. Caudate lobe is the only part of liver related to lesser sac. Lesser omentum attaches at fissure for ligamentum venosum. From stomach, lesser omentum goes upward to attach to liver. In its free margin, lie the structures: DAV → ducts, artery, vein (hepatic ducts, hepatic artery, portal vein)—plus lymphatics and nerves. Behind its free margin lies the epiploic foramen (of Winslow)—bounded by caudate lobe above, 1st part of duodenum below, IVC posteriorly, and hepatoduodenal ligament anteriorly. Very important surgically. Why? Because compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament here (Pringle’s maneuver) occludes portal triad and reduces blood loss during hepatectomy. Posterior surface also shows groove for oesophagus. Now come to inferior surface (visceral surface): related to stomach, pylorus, gall bladder, duodenum, colon, right kidney—all covered by peritoneum. Non-peritoneal areas are: fissure of ligamentum teres, porta hepatis, gall bladder fossa. Porta hepatis: gateway of liver. Entry and exit for structures. Hepatic ducts → bile drainage (form R & L hepatic ducts, join to form common hepatic duct, + cystic duct = common bile duct). Hepatic artery → branch of common hepatic (→ hepatic proper). At porta divides into right & left. Right hepatic artery gives cystic artery. Portal vein → enters and divides into right & left at porta. Right branch supplies segments 5,6,7,8; left branch supplies 2,3,4. Variations are common—sometimes trifurcation, sometimes absent branches. Gall bladder: covered by peritoneum, but its bed (where it contacts liver) is bare. Contains deep branch of cystic artery and vein. Here lies Calot’s triangle (cystohepatic triangle)—bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct, liver margin. Contains cystic artery, lymph nodes, ducts. Key landmark in cholecystectomy. Must be dissected carefully to avoid injury. Finally, understand subphrenic spaces: suprahepatic (right & left), infrahepatic (including right hepatorenal pouch of Morrison, and left lesser sac). Morrison’s pouch = most dependent part of peritoneal cavity when lying down. Very common site for subphrenic abscess—clinically relevant in liver surgery. So what did we learn? Anatomical lobes (right, left, caudate, quadrate). Functional lobes by Cantlie’s line. Sectors & Couinaud’s segments. Hepatic, portal, biliary relations. Surgical landmarks: hepatoduodenal ligament, Pringle’s maneuver, Calot’s triangle, Morrison’s pouch. This is crucial surgical anatomy for liver transplant and liver surgeries. Hello my dear students. Today we are going to discuss the anatomy of the liver. The liver, being such a peculiar organ, often kind of stumps you. Let’s make it easy, because it may seem difficult, but it is very, very relevant. We really need to learn it before we go any further. 

You should know the basic anatomy of the liver, you should know its microscopic structure, which is covered in a separate lecture, and you should know about portal-caval anastomosis, Couinaud’s segments, portal vein, hepatorenal pouch of Morrison, peritoneal spaces, and surgical anatomy of the liver from the point of view of liver surgery. All of this is covered in separate lectures. Once you have the anatomy in place, you can quickly jump into those shorter lectures and understand them easily. Again, remember—study and move forward.

Right. So, the liver—where is it? The liver is a wedge-shaped organ present in the upper right corner of the abdomen. It performs both endocrine and exocrine functions. I am sure you know that exocrine function means production of bile. Endocrine functions are many. Just remember that it is a very important part of your metabolism—of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, hormones, and so on. All metabolic activities happen in the liver. This results in generation of some amount of heat, so regulation of body temperature is also one of the functions of the liver.

Now let us come to its anatomy. Where is it situated? Think of those nine abdominal regions that you have studied. The liver is present in the right hypochondrium, epigastrium, and a little bit in the left hypochondrium. It is covered by the 7th to 11th ribs and intercostal spaces. It is wedge-shaped, and this wedge-shaped organ has five surfaces: anterior, superior, posterior, inferior, and right lateral. Look at the wedge and recognize this: here is the anterior surface, this is the superior, this is posterior, this is inferior, and this is right lateral. Very easy—simply anterior, superior, posterior, inferior, right lateral.

Then they are separated by certain borders. Just remember one thing: not all borders are clearly visualized, that is the challenge. There are only three borders that are somewhat well visualized. The inferior border is very sharp and well visualized. It separates anterior from inferior surface. Then there is the posterosuperior border separating superior from posterior surface, and the posteroinferior border separating posterior from inferior. The others are not needed, so don’t bother with them.

A common exam question: place the organ in its normal anatomical position. Imagine you pick up this wedge liver—the smaller end should come to the left, the larger part to the right. Keep the sharpest border (inferior) facing downwards. Place the bare area posteriorly to the right. You will find a groove for inferior vena cava posteriorly; insert a forceps vertically through it. If you are able to do that, your liver is in the right position. The right lobe will be slightly higher than the left.

What is the normal weight of the liver? In an adult male, it is 1.4 to 1.8 kilograms. In females, slightly less, about 1.2 to 1.4 kilograms. It is relevant—you should understand how much proportion of the body weight is liver. In a newborn it is 1/10 of body weight; in an adult, 1/36th. So as you grow, the liver comparatively reduces in proportion. These are often asked in exams and vivas.

How do we study it? Liver is always studied by surfaces, borders, lobes, and fissures. So that is how I will teach here. Surfaces can be divided into parietal and visceral. Parietal—those related to body wall (anterior, superior, posterior, right lateral). Visceral—those related to other organs, like stomach, duodenum, colon, right kidney, gall bladder. Imagine the liver in your body and visualize—do not just mug it up.

Let’s start with the superior surface. Below your lung is the diaphragm; below the right dome of diaphragm is liver. The superior surface is higher on the right than the left. Behind it is the IVC. The falciform ligament attaches to the anterior surface, dividing into two layers, one to the left forming the left triangular ligament, and one to the right forming superior layer of coronary ligament. Together these form the posterosuperior border. The superior surface is related to the lung and pleura.

Now to the right lateral surface—related laterally to ribs and body wall. Till 8th rib it is related to right lung, till 10th rib to costodiaphragmatic recess. Below that, directly with diaphragm. Why does it matter? Because in liver biopsy, you must avoid injury to lung. So the needle is inserted below 8th rib—in 9th or 10th intercostal space, in midaxillary line, during expiration so that lung moves up.

Anterior surface: covered by ribs (right 6th–10th ribs, left 7th and 8th cartilages), related to xiphoid process. Here falciform ligament attaches anteriorly. The falciform ligament is a double fold of peritoneum, extending from umbilicus to lower liver border. In its free margin: obliterated left umbilical vein (ligamentum teres hepatis) and paraumbilical veins. These paraumbilical veins connect portal venous system and systemic veins—site of portocaval anastomosis. The left umbilical vein originally carried oxygenated foetal blood from placenta to liver. After birth, it obliterates, forming ligamentum teres hepatis. The ductus venosus, which bypassed foetal liver, becomes ligamentum venosum. Together with falciform ligament, these divide liver anatomically into a very large right lobe (5/6th) and a small left lobe (1/6th).

Posteriorly you see caudate and quadrate lobes, both considered part of anatomical right lobe. Posterior surface: bounded by posterosuperior and posteroinferior borders. From right to left: bare area (not covered by peritoneum, bounded by coronary ligament layers, related to right adrenal gland, kidney, diaphragm, site for portocaval anastomosis), groove for inferior vena cava (with hepatic veins opening), caudate lobe (between IVC groove and ligamentum venosum fissure), ligamentum venosum, and groove for oesophagus. Special features include Spigelian lobe, papillary process. Caudate lobe is unique in being related to lesser sac.

Inferior (visceral) surface lies between posteroinferior and sharp inferior borders. Inferior border has notch for ligamentum teres left of midline and gall bladder notch on right. Inferior surface relations: stomach, pylorus, duodenum, colon, right kidney (all peritoneal); gall bladder bed (non-peritoneal). Porta hepatis is here—it is the gateway to liver. Structures entering liver: portal vein (75% supply), hepatic artery (25%), nerves. Leaving: hepatic ducts, lymphatics. Remember the mnemonic DAV (duct, artery, vein).

Quadrate lobe is bounded by fissure for ligamentum teres on left, gall bladder fossa on right, porta hepatis above, inferior border below. Non-peritoneal areas include porta hepatis, gall bladder fossa, fissure for ligamentum teres. Ligaments: falciform, coronary, right and left triangular, lesser omentum—all peritoneal folds, called “false” ligaments. True ligaments are ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum, remnants of foetal veins.

Now blood supply. Liver receives 75% of blood from portal vein, 25% from hepatic artery. Venous drainage through hepatic veins into IVC. Hepatic artery arises from celiac trunk via common hepatic artery → hepatic artery proper → right and left branches. Right hepatic artery gives cystic artery. Portal vein is formed by union of superior mesenteric and splenic veins behind neck of pancreas. It receives left gastric (oesophageal tributaries), right gastric, paraumbilical, cystic vein. All blood eventually drains into portal vein → branches in liver sinusoids → central vein → hepatic veins (right, middle, left) → IVC.

Now functional division. Anatomically, caudate and quadrate lobes belong to right lobe. But functionally, by Cantlie’s line (line from gall bladder to IVC along middle hepatic vein), liver is divided into right and left functional lobes. Right lobe is further divided by right hepatic vein into anterior and posterior sectors; left lobe by left hepatic vein into medial and lateral sectors. Within sectors, Couinaud described 8 segments—each with its own portal inflow, hepatic arterial supply, hepatic venous drainage, and bile duct. Thus each segment is surgically resectable independently. Segments: 1=caudate, 2&3=left lateral, 4a&4b=left medial, 5&8=right anterior (inferior and superior), 6&7=right posterior (inferior and superior).

Nerve supply is from hepatic plexus (sympathetic and parasympathetic). Lymphatics from superficial and deep groups drain to hepatic, celiac, phrenic, and paracardial nodes. Support: though people say ligaments support liver, actually the main support is hepatic veins anchoring liver to IVC. Intra-abdominal pressure and surrounding viscera also help. Liver “hangs” in abdomen, not resting on bone.

So in conclusion, we have studied surfaces, borders, lobes, fissures, ligaments, blood supply, venous drainage, functional and segmental anatomy, nerve and lymphatic supply, supports, and clinical points. The rest—portal vein, portocaval anastomosis, Couinaud segments, surgical anatomy—are covered separately. Again remember, MCQs and notes for this lecture are available as handouts. If you need the written word to study you can access it there. If you liked the lecture, please like, subscribe, and share with friends. Origin and Early Branches First, imagine and draw the stylomastoid foramen—this is the point where the facial nerve exits the skull. As soon as the facial nerve emerges from the stylomastoid foramen, it gives off some early branches: The posterior auricular nerve → supplies the occipitalis and posterior auricular muscles. A branch to the posterior belly of digastric muscle. A branch to the stylohyoid muscle. Entry into the Parotid Gland After this, the facial nerve enters the parotid gland. Inside the parotid gland, it divides into two major divisions: Temporofacial division Cervicofacial division. Temporofacial Division The temporofacial division further splits into: Temporal branch Zygomatic branch Temporal branch supplies: Auricular muscles (superior and anterior), Frontalis muscle, Corrugator supercilii, Procerus, Upper part of orbicularis oculi. Zygomatic branch also contributes to orbicularis oculi, thus completing innervation of muscles around the orbit. Cervicofacial Division The cervicofacial division splits into three branches: Buccal branch Marginal mandibular branch Cervical branch Buccal branch: divides into upper and lower divisions. Upper buccal → supplies muscles of the upper lip: levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris, zygomaticus minor, zygomaticus major, levator anguli oris. Lower buccal → supplies buccinator and orbicularis oris (muscles of cheek and lip). Marginal mandibular branch: supplies muscles along the lower lip and chin: depressor labii inferioris, depressor anguli oris, and risorius. Cervical branch: descends into the neck to supply the platysma (the large superficial neck muscle). Overview at the Parotid To give a better perspective, draw the parotid gland. You can now show how the facial nerve enters this gland, divides, and emerges from its anterior border in the form of the five terminal branches: From above downwards: Temporal Zygomatic Buccal Marginal mandibular Cervical This arrangement is often remembered as: “Two Zebras Bit My Cheek.” Key Point Thus, the facial nerve supplies all the muscles of facial expression, through its five terminal branches, plus some additional branches given off earlier (posterior auricular, digastric, stylohyoid). So to summarise: Exit from stylomastoid foramen → early branches. Entry into parotid gland → divisions into temporofacial & cervicofacial. Final anterior parotid border → five terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical.

Any first MBBS student, a third MBBS student studying surgery, a student doing post-graduation in surgery, ENT, ophthalmology, obstetrics and gynaecology, or any specialist in the field of surgery will benefit from this surgical anatomy series. Remember, if you like the lecture, the notes are present in the form of handouts. You can go there and regularly go through the content in handout format. So let’s begin this lecture on anorectal surgery – developmental and anatomical perspectives. How is this lecture planned? First, we will discuss the development of rectum and anal canal in brief, then the anatomy of rectum, then the anatomy of anal canal along with discussion of venous drainage, haemorrhoids, fistula, and all other anatomy through which we will present surgical relevance as and when it is important. Let’s first discuss development of rectum. So let us ask ourselves a real clinical situation. Imagine a female infant is born with a small dimple where the anus should be. On examining her vagina, the presence of meconium was seen. Radiographic exploration showed that there was a tiny little tract communicating backward into the vagina. The question is: with which part of the lower bowel would the fistula probably be connected? From the image we can see that it is connected to the rectum. Can you name this birth defect? Yes, we know that it is a rectovaginal fistula. But what is the embryological basis for this condition? Why did this happen? To understand that, let’s understand the development. Imagine a developing embryo. In the developing embryo, there is a hind-gut, which reaches the surface at the cloacal membrane. The hind-gut is attached to the posterior abdominal wall via a dorsal mesentery which contains the inferior mesenteric artery, the artery of the hind-gut. The hind-gut tube reaches the cloacal membrane which is made of endoderm and ectoderm with no mesoderm in between. Adjacent to this is the allantois, a diverticulum of the hind-gut, entering the umbilicus. At the point where the allantois attaches to the hind-gut, the hind-gut is divided into a pre-allantoic part and a post-allantoic part. Now, what develops from the pre-allantoic hind-gut? From this portion of hind-gut, the left one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum up to the middle rectal valve develops. This means that till the middle rectal valve, it is all endodermal in origin from the pre-allantoic hind-gut. What develops from the post-allantoic part? From this part develops the rest of the rectum below the middle rectal valve, the upper part of anal canal, and surprisingly also the urinary bladder. How does gut tube develop the urinary bladder? Because the post-allantoic hind-gut dilates to form the endodermal cloaca, which then reaches the surface at the cloacal membrane. Over time the cloacal membrane, which initially faces forward, shifts to face downward as the body wall lengthens and perineum forms. A surface depression also develops, called the proctodeum. Now, from above we have the endodermal cloaca, from below the ectodermal proctodeum. Between the hind-gut and allantois, a septum grows downward – the urorectal septum. This divides the cloaca into two: anterior primitive urogenital sinus (future bladder, urethra) and posterior primitive rectum (future rectum and anal canal). The short communication between them before septum completes is called the “cloacal duct.” If cloacal duct is not obliterated, fistulas persist—like rectovaginal, rectourethral fistula, etc. The urorectal septum has three components: a vertical part and two lateral ridges. As the lateral components grow inward, they bring along the paramesonephric ducts (future uterus in females). That is why the uterus lies between bladder in front and rectum behind. The urorectal septum fuses with cloacal membrane, dividing it into a urogenital membrane and an anal membrane. The ectodermal proctodeum pushes in and forms the anal pit. This is separated from the rectum above by the anal membrane. Finally, the anal membrane ruptures—its site is marked by the pectinate line. Thus, above the pectinate line, anal canal is endodermal in origin; below the pectinate line, it is ectodermal in origin. Functionally and clinically this pectinate line is important: above it, blood supply is via superior rectal artery (branch of IMA), venous drainage into portal system, lymph to inferior mesenteric nodes, nerve supply autonomic (hence insensitive). Below it, blood supply via inferior rectal artery (branch of internal pudendal), venous drainage into systemic veins, lymph to superficial inguinal nodes, nerve supply somatic (inferior rectal nerve), hence very sensitive to pain. Therefore, development explains both the anatomy and clinical features such as the spread of tumors and differences in pain sensitivity. Tumors above pectinate line metastasize via portal route to liver; those below metastasize to systemic sites like lungs. Developmental anomalies arise if steps fail. For example: persistent anal membrane leads to imperforate anus; shallow proctodeum causes anoperineal fistula; incompletely formed urorectal septum results in rectovaginal and rectourethral fistulas; failure of migration of neural crest into distal gut causes Hirschsprung’s disease with aganglionic, non-peristaltic bowel segment. So, coming back—rectovaginal fistula embryologic basis is persistence of cloacal duct due to failure of complete urorectal septum development, particularly the lateral components. Now let’s turn to the gross anatomy of rectum and anal canal. Rectum, though name suggests straight tube, is not straight in humans. It begins at rectosigmoid junction at S3 and ends at anorectal junction passing through pelvic diaphragm to anal canal. It lies anterior to sacrum and coccyx, measures 13–14 cm long, dilated in its lower part (rectal ampulla). It has anterior-posterior curvature and lateral curvatures. It is partly covered by peritoneum: upper third on all sides, middle third only in front, lower third not at all. In males, peritoneal reflection forms rectovesical pouch; in females, rectouterine pouch. The non-peritoneal lower part is separated by fascia – rectovesical fascia (Denonvillier’s fascia) in males, rectovaginal fascia in females. Posteriorly rectum relates to sacrum, coccyx, vessels and nerves; laterally to pelvic muscles and vessels, with important pararectal space and lateral ligaments carrying middle rectal vessels. Rectum is held by supports: puborectalis sling, fascia, ligaments, pelvic floor, perineal body; loss of support causes prolapse. Rectal mucosa shows permanent transverse folds, called valves of Houston (usually three), the most important being the middle rectal valve on right anterior wall—it retains faeces till evacuation. Important clinical points: per rectal examination in males allows palpation of prostate, seminal vesicles, etc.; in females, cervix and uterus. Now the anal canal. It extends about 3.8 cm from anorectal junction to anal orifice. It is closed most of the time. It is surrounded by sphincter muscles: internal sphincter (thickened smooth muscle, involuntary) and external sphincter (skeletal, voluntary, with deep, superficial, and subcutaneous parts). Together with puborectalis, they form anorectal ring essential for continence. Within anal canal wall is the submucosal venous plexus, both internal and external, connecting portal and systemic systems, thus a major site of porto-caval anastomosis. Engorgement causes haemorrhoids. Internal haemorrhoids (above pectinate line, painless) vs external haemorrhoids (below, painful). Primary piles occur at 3, 7, and 11 o’clock positions (lithotomy position). Internally the mucosa forms longitudinal ridges—the anal columns of Morgagni—with intervening anal valves and sinuses, the line of these is the pectinate line. Above it: endodermal, portal drainage, autonomic innervation. Below it: ectodermal, systemic drainage, somatic innervation. Surrounding glands and crypts can become infected leading to abscess and fistula. Anal fistulas are abnormal tracts from anal canal lumen to perianal skin. Types include intersphincteric, trans-sphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric, and submucosal, depending on relationship to sphincters. So to summarize: the pectinate line marks a watershed in development, blood supply, nerve supply, lymphatic drainage, tumour spread, surgical anatomy and clinical conditions of rectum and anal canal. Thus today we discussed the development of rectum and anal canal, their gross and internal anatomy, venous drainage, haemorrhoids, anal fistula, and the surgical relevance of all these. Thank you, and we’ll see you across the screen in the next surgical anatomy lecture.

Hello my dear students. We are continuing our midbrain series. Today, we are going to study the crus cerebri and the substantia nigra in detail. When we look at the brainstem from the posterior side, we know it can be sectioned at two levels: at the level of the superior colliculus and at the level of the inferior colliculus. These two sections together help us understand most of the structure and function of the midbrain. As I always suggest, please take a neat drawing book or digital drawing tool, add a heading, and start sketching with me. Remember—the substantia nigra and the crus cerebri are common to both the superior and inferior collicular sections. That’s why we study them first, because we will encounter them again later. So draw: in the middle is the aqueduct of Sylvius, the central cavity of the midbrain. Around it lies the periaqueductal gray. Everything in front of the aqueduct is the cerebral peduncle, and everything behind is the tectum. Now in front of the tegmentum, we draw a dark band—the substantia nigra. In front of substantia nigra lies a thick bundle of longitudinal fibers—the crus cerebri. That is today’s focus. The cerebral peduncle consists of crus cerebri, substantia nigra, tegmentum, and periaqueductal gray. The tectum lies posterior to the aqueduct. So in each section of the midbrain, remember: posteriorly, tectum; anteriorly, cerebral peduncle, which itself has crus, substantia nigra, tegmentum, and periaqueductal gray. Now let’s zoom in on the crus cerebri. Crus cerebri is made of corticofugal fibers—fibers descending from the cortex to brainstem and spinal cord. They are arranged as: medial 1/6th, middle 2/3rds, and lateral 1/6th. Middle 2/3rds: contain corticospinal fibers (to spinal cord) and corticobulbar fibers (to cranial nerve nuclei in brainstem). Medial 1/6th: frontopontine fibers (frontal lobe to pons). Lateral 1/6th: temporopontine, parietopontine, occipitopontine fibers (from temporal, parietal, occipital lobes to pons). So essentially all lobes of the cortex send fibers to the pons. These form the corticopontocerebellar pathway: cortex → pons → opposite cerebellum (through pontocerebellar fibers). This is how the cerebellum is constantly informed about intended motor actions of the opposite cerebral cortex. Now the substantia nigra. It is a dark band of neurons lying between tegmentum and crus cerebri. It appears dark because of high melanin content. It is convex in shape, thicker medially. Classically, it has two parts: Pars compacta (dorsal): densely packed cells, high melanin, produces dopamine. Pars reticulata (ventral): loosely packed, high iron content, lighter appearance. Some of its fibers even intermingle with crus cerebri fibers. Now the connections of substantia nigra: From corpus striatum (caudate and lentiform nuclei) to substantia nigra: fibers called striatonigral fibers, carrying GABA (inhibitory). From substantia nigra pars compacta back to striatum: fibers called nigrostriatal fibers, carrying dopamine (also inhibitory). So note: striatum inhibits substantia nigra, and substantia nigra inhibits striatum. They are mutually inhibitory, maintaining balance. Some fibers also go to thalamus (nigrothalamic). Why is this important? Because substantia nigra integrates cortical and basal ganglia signals and regulates voluntary movements. It suppresses the tendency of basal ganglia to produce uncontrolled movements, ensuring smooth, purposeful motor activity. Dopamine is the key neurotransmitter. Now, when substantia nigra degenerates, as in Parkinson’s disease, dopamine production falls. The striatum is no longer inhibited, so uncontrolled activity emerges, producing the symptoms of Parkinsonism. Symptoms of Parkinsonism: Resting tremors: the classic “shaking even when sitting still,” unlike cerebellar intention tremor. Pill-rolling movements: fingers and thumb roll imaginary pills constantly. Cogwheel rigidity: when passively moving a limb, there is intermittent resistance in a ratchety fashion. This differs from “clasp-knife rigidity” seen in UMN lesions. Mask-like face: lack of expression. Shuffling gait: short steps, stiff joints, difficulty stopping movement, stooped posture. Sometimes the patient suddenly breaks into a little run because he cannot stop. Bradykinesia: difficulty initiating and terminating movement. These are the classic motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease. In class, I often demonstrate them to students—for example, stooping forward, showing tremoring hands, pill-rolling, slow shuffling gait. This helps them memorize easily. So to summarize today’s lecture: we focused on crus cerebri and substantia nigra. Crus cerebri: descending corticofugal fibers, arranged in medial (frontopontine), middle (corticospinal + corticobulbar), and lateral (occipitopontine + parietopontine + temporopontine). Substantia nigra: pars compacta (dopamine, dense cells), pars reticulata (iron, sparse cells). Its connections with striatum form an inhibitory loop. Degeneration causes Parkinsonism with resting tremor, pill-rolling, cogwheel rigidity, mask-like face, shuffling gait, stooped posture, bradykinesia. I hope you enjoyed this lecture and understood it well. Remember: you must know midbrain structures thoroughly to understand conditions like Parkinsonism. See you across the screen in the next lecture on midbrain at the level of inferior colliculus. Thank you.

Hello my dear friends. Today we are studying the Midbrain. Specifically, we are going to look at the midbrain at the level of the Inferior Colliculus. When we look at the brainstem from behind, we can section it at two levels: one at the superior colliculus, and one at the inferior colliculus. In this lecture, we are at the lower section, at the level of the Inferior Colliculus. As usual, let us begin with what we already know. In neuroanatomy, it helps to first recall the basics. You already know the overall shape of the midbrain section. You know the crus cerebri. You know the substantia nigra. These are common structures in both superior and inferior colliculus sections, so you should be able to draw them confidently now. So begin your diagram: one half of the midbrain, then the other half, separated by the aqueduct of Sylvius. Around the aqueduct, draw a circle to represent the periaqueductal gray matter. Then draw two thick lines—thicker medially and thinner laterally—for the substantia nigra. In front of the substantia nigra lies the crus cerebri. Behind it lies the tegmentum, and around the aqueduct lies the periaqueductal gray. Posterior to all this is the tectum. These are the compartments you have seen before: crus cerebri anteriorly, substantia nigra behind it, tegmentum posterior to substantia nigra, periaqueductal gray around the aqueduct, and tectum forming the posterior part. So far we have just revised known structures. Today’s focus will be on the tegmentum, the periaqueductal gray, and the tectum at the level of the inferior colliculus. In the tegmentum, the first thing to add is the lemniscal band. You might remember learning this at the level of the pons too. There are four longitudinal tracts here: The medial lemniscus which carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the opposite side of the body (since fibers crossed as internal arcuate fibers at medulla). The trigeminal lemniscus, which carries pain, temperature from the spinal nucleus of trigeminal and touch/pressure from the principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal, all to the thalamus, representing the opposite half of the face. The spinal lemniscus, which carries pain and temperature from the opposite half of the body. The lateral lemniscus, which carries auditory impulses from cochlear nuclei. So the lemniscal band has shifted slightly laterally and posteriorly as compared to the pons. Always remember the origin: medial lemniscus = dorsal column pathway, trigeminal = face sensory pathways, spinal lemniscus = spinothalamic tracts, and lateral lemniscus = auditory fibers. Now, add the trochlear nerve nucleus in the periaqueductal gray. The trochlear nerve emerges from this nucleus, but fibers take a special route: they cross dorsally, wind around the midbrain, and then come forward. This makes the trochlear nerve unique: it is the only cranial nerve to emerge dorsally and to undergo complete decussation. Functionally, it carries general somatic efferent fibers to one extraocular muscle—the superior oblique muscle. Add also the RTM tracts (present near midline): Rubrospinal tract: a descending, extrapyramidal pathway, facilitating flexors and inhibiting extensors. Tectospinal tract: mediates reflex movements of head and body in response to visual stimuli. Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF): connects vestibular nuclei to cranial nerves, coordinating conjugate eye movements with head movement. Next, add the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the periaqueductal gray. Note that this is unusual—it contains first-order sensory neurons within the CNS (most first-order sensory neurons lie in ganglia outside CNS). This nucleus deals with proprioception from the face and jaw. Now we move to the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation. At the level of inferior colliculus, you see fibers of superior cerebellar peduncle crossing in the midline. The cerebellum receives information from the opposite cortex (via corticopontocerebellar fibers) and sends its efferents back through dentatothalamic and cerebellorubral fibers. They cross in the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation, go to the opposite red nucleus and thalamus, and then back to the opposite cerebral cortex, completing the circuit. Also recall the ventral spinocerebellar tract fibers: they cross twice (first at the spinal cord, then once again through superior cerebellar peduncle), finally entering the cerebellum on the ipsilateral side. Now let’s add the last big feature of this section: the tectum, specifically the nucleus of the inferior colliculus. Place it adjacent to the lateral lemniscus and connect it via the inferior brachium to the medial geniculate body. From the medial geniculate, fibers ascend to the primary auditory cortex in temporal lobe. So the pathway for hearing is: cochlear nerve → cochlear nuclei → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → inferior brachium → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex. Thus, the inferior colliculus acts as a lower auditory center. The inferior colliculus also informs the superior colliculus for audio-visual coordination (for example, in a dark room if you hear a sound, your eyes automatically turn toward the source). It also communicates with the opposite inferior colliculus, allowing bilateral auditory integration. Auditory modulation also occurs here: descending corticofugal fibers can suppress background sounds and enhance relevant sounds—for example, in a noisy crowd you can still clearly hear your friend’s voice. That selective attention is possible because of these modulating descending tracts. So, to summarize: at the level of the inferior colliculus section of midbrain, we have studied substantia nigra and crus cerebri (already known), then the lemniscal band (medial, trigeminal, spinal, lateral), the trochlear nucleus, RTM tracts, mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal, superior cerebellar peduncle decussation, and finally tectum with the nucleus of the inferior colliculus and its auditory connections. What is left? We will continue with the section at the level of superior colliculus in the next lecture. Please revise this lecture, solve the MCQs at the end, and remember to check any notes attached—I may leave additional points in note section even if I don’t fully explain in video. See you in the next lecture on the section at the level of superior colliculus. Bye.

Hello my dear students. I have been teaching anatomy for the last 25 years, and I love it. This lecture is part of my Central Nervous System lecture series, but specifically it is an MCQ series. By now, I assume you know your spinal cord anatomy well, because I have taken so many lectures on the spinal cord—on microscopic structure, tracts, lesions, blood supply. Today it is time to test that knowledge with MCQs. I have a method of solving MCQs. I divide any topic into groups: spinal cord blood supply, spinal cord lesions, spinal cord tracts, etc. I have already done Spinal Cord MCQs Part 1, which consisted of microscopic structure and development—on which many questions are asked. Today we are on Spinal Cord MCQs Part 2. Please pause and read the instructions: When we solve MCQs, we do not just give the answer but also explain why A is correct, why B, C, and D are not. Simultaneously, I also give you notes in either writing or image form so you can revise them later. The idea is that while solving MCQs you are also studying the subject in depth. Next time, when you’re in a hurry, you can just pick up notes and remember. The aim is always: solve MCQs while studying. That way you’re both learning method of solving and strengthening your concepts. So, let’s begin. This part consists of MCQs on Upper Motor Neuron vs Lower Motor Neuron, pyramidal vs extra-pyramidal tracts, and spinal cord syndromes like Brown Sequard and Central Cord. 

MCQ 1: “Lesions of the following structures would result in UMN lesion, EXCEPT.” Options: internal capsule, motor cortex, lateral corticospinal tract, first thoracic nerve. The first three are UMN structures. The first thoracic spinal nerve is a peripheral nerve, so lesion here produces LMN features. Therefore, correct answer is first thoracic nerve.

MCQ 2: “Following statements are true about UMN and LMN lesions, except.” Damage to internal capsule → UMN lesion. Small central lesion in spinal cord → no UMN or LMN lesion, since it is too central. Degerin’s syndrome (medullary lesion involving pyramid + hypoglossal nerve) → produces UMN lesion and LMN lesion simultaneously. Damage to anterior horn of spinal cord → LMN lesion. So the false statement is: small central spinal cord lesion produces both. Now an example: In medial medullary syndrome, the pyramid is damaged (UMN lesion) and hypoglossal nerve is damaged (LMN lesion).

MCQ 3: “Which tract is a pyramidal tract?” Answer: corticospinal tract. The others (rubrospinal, vestibulospinal) are extra-pyramidal; spinothalamic is ascending.

MCQ 4: “Following is true about pyramidal tract, except.” About one-third fibers arise from sensory cortex. Somatotopic organization in internal capsule is head-toe, anterior to posterior. Fibers decussate in lower medulla. In lateral corticospinal tract, arrangement is sacral to cervical from medial to lateral (actually it is cervical medial → sacral lateral, not the other way). So the incorrect statement is sacral-medial to cervical-lateral.

MCQ 5: Disassociated anaesthesia is seen in? Answer: syringomyelia. Syringomyelia is a cavitating lesion in central spinal cord damaging crossing spinothalamic (pain-temp) fibers while sparing dorsal column → pain lost, touch preserved.

MCQ 6: “All are extra-pyramidal tracts except.” Pyramidal tract is corticospinal. So answer is lateral corticospinal tract. Extra-pyramidal tracts include rubrospinal, tectospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, medial longitudinal fasciculus etc.

MCQ 7: “Following pairs are correct EXCEPT.” Tectospinal tract—audio-visual reflex. Vestibulospinal—balance. Rubrospinal—body alertness (false; rubric → movement, flexor facilitation). Pyramidal (corticospinal)—fine motor control. So incorrect pair is rubrospinal = alertness.

MCQ 8: “Decussation of red nucleus fibers is called?” Answer: decussation of Forel (ventral tegmental decussation).

MCQ 9: Interesting MCQ: “A young lady about to cross the road hears a loud truck horn and quickly turns her head to look.” This is an audio-visual reflex—mediated by tectospinal tract.

MCQ 10: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) connects which cranial nerves? It connects nuclei of 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 12th cranial nerves and upper cervical spinal nerves. It does not include V (trigeminal).

MCQ 11: “Following is true in lower motor neuron lesion.” LMN lesion shows flaccid paralysis with muscle atrophy. UMN lesion would cause spasticity, Babinski’s sign, brisk reflexes.

MCQ 12: Lesion of right internal capsule would cause left-sided deficits (contralateral hemiplegia, UMN features, hemianesthesia). But it will not cause LMN paralysis because cranial/spinal nerves themselves are intact.

MCQ 13: “Brown Sequard syndrome (hemisection of cord)”—what statement is incorrect? Brown Sequard results in ipsilateral UMN paralysis, ipsilateral loss of fine touch, contralateral loss of pain/temp below lesion. Therefore, incorrect is “contralateral UMN lesion.”

MCQ 14: “Complete cord transection at thoracic level”—bilateral UMN paralysis, complete anesthesia, loss of bowel/bladder function. The statement that bladder/bowel function is preserved is false.

MCQ 15: “Anterior cord syndrome” results from anterior cord damage—bilateral spastic paralysis, loss of pain/temp, LMN signs at lesion level. But dorsal columns intact, so fine touch is preserved. So the incorrect statement was “loss of touch.”

MCQ 16: “Central cord syndrome”—common in cervical syringomyelia. Produces dissociated anesthesia, loss of upper limb motor more than lower; “sacral sparing” because sacral fibers lie peripheral. The incorrect statement given was “no loss of pain”—false, pain is lost.

MCQ 17: Polio—destroys anterior horn motor neurons → LMN paralysis. So answer: damage to motor neurons in anterior grey horn.

MCQ 18: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)—affects motor system (both UMN and LMN). Classically corticospinal tracts are affected.

MCQ 19: Ascending vs descending tracts. Ascending tracts lie in white matter and carry sensory impulses. Descending tracts lie in white matter and carry motor impulses. The wrong statement was that descending lie in grey. Answer: ascending = white sensory, descending = white motor.

MCQ 20: “Characteristic pattern of Brown Sequard syndrome.” It is contralateral loss of pain and temperature, and ipsilateral loss of motor and fine touch below level of lesion. That is the classical picture.

MCQ 21: “Multiple sclerosis”—a demyelinating disease of CNS. Which cells are affected? Oligodendrocytes, because they myelinate CNS. Thus with this, we complete Spinal Cord MCQ Part 2. Hello my dear students. For the last month, I have been teaching you the topic of fertilization. Today, I assume you have studied it well, and now I am going to take you through MCQs based on fertilization. Think of it as a test for you to see how much you have understood. At our institution, the way we teach MCQs is as follows: First, try and answer on your own without looking at the options. Then, when you look at the options, begin eliminating the obviously wrong ones. Often you will be left with two possibilities—that is where you need to focus. Also always check whether the MCQ is asking “EXCEPT” (looking for the wrong option) or “TRUE” (looking for the right option). That habit will keep you alert in the game. And remember, only practice, practice, practice is going to take you to the level where you can solve MCQs confidently. Of course, you must also have studied the topic well. So what we do here is: we will solve the MCQ together, we will discuss why option A, B, C, or D is correct or incorrect, and simultaneously I will give you notes. On your screen, you will often see a note icon pop up. That note is something for you to revise later—so next time, if you don’t have time to watch the whole explanation, you can simply go through the notes and solve quickly. The aim is both to solve MCQs and to study additional information that becomes useful later. Now let’s begin. MCQ 1. In which stage do you first see haploid chromosomal number? The options are spermatogonia, primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes, or none. Spermatogonia are diploid. They give rise to primary spermatocytes—again diploid. Primary spermatocyte enters meiosis I, which is a reduction division. So the product is secondary spermatocyte, which is now haploid. Thus, haploid number appears in secondary spermatocyte. Correct answer: secondary spermatocytes. MCQ 2. Which sperm chromosome travels faster – X or Y? This was asked in a previous exam, phrased as “sperm chromosome faster.” The answer: Y chromosome sperm travels faster. MCQ 3. Which changes are seen during capacitation of sperm, EXCEPT? Capacitation is the conditioning process sperm undergo in female tract. It involves removal of glycoprotein coat and plasma proteins, increase in calcium permeability, cholesterol removal, and enhanced motility. So if any option says “decreased calcium permeability,” that is incorrect. Thus, correct answer: decrease in calcium permeability is NOT seen. Another MCQ here: Time required for capacitation is about 7 hours. So if options include 2, 3, 5, 7 hours—the right one is 7 hours. MCQ 5. Site of spermatogenesis? Options: epididymis, seminiferous tubule, ductus deferens, prostate. Sperms are produced only in seminiferous tubules. Epididymis is where they mature, not where they are produced. So answer is seminiferous tubules. MCQ 6. All are true about seminal vesicles EXCEPT? They produce a secretion rich in fructose, lie beside the prostate, and give mucous content to semen. But they do not store sperms. So the false statement is “seminal vesicles store sperms.” MCQ 7. Major contribution to seminal fluid comes from: It is the seminal vesicles. The prostate also contributes but lesser. Most volume of semen fluid is from seminal vesicles. MCQ 8. Spermatogenesis begins at: It begins at puberty in males. In females, oogenesis begins during intrauterine life. MCQ 9. Oogenesis begins when? In females, oogenesis begins before birth—around seventh month of intrauterine life, when primary oocytes enter meiosis I and arrest at diplotene stage. So the answer is “before birth.” MCQ 10. Where do sperms attain maturity? Though there are multiple opinions, the answer is: in epididymis. There they gain motility and full maturation. MCQ 11. Time taken for liquefaction of semen? It takes about 30 minutes. Initially semen coagulates; enzymes then liquefy it in about 30 minutes, which helps sperm motility. MCQ 12. Which cells lie outside “blood-testis barrier”? The answer: Leydig cells. Sertoli cells form the barrier inside seminiferous tubules, dividing the basal and adluminal compartments to protect germ cells. Leydig cells lie outside this barrier. MCQ 13. Axial filament of sperm tail has which arrangement? It shows the classical 9 + 2 microtubule arrangement (nine doublets around, two central singlets). MCQ 14. Normal sperm count? Normal is around 60–120 million per ml. Lesser values are abnormal. MCQ 15. In semen analysis of an infertile male, absence of sperms indicates: If due to mumps orchitis, some spermatogenesis occurs though reduced. A count of zero (azoospermia) is usually due to obstruction in the duct system. So correct cause: blocked ducts. MCQ 16. Artificial insemination using husband’s semen is indicated in: Oligozoospermia (low count), impotence (but sperms viable), antisperm antibodies in cervical mucus (overcome by directly inserting sperm). But not in azoospermia (zero sperm). So azoospermia is the contraindication. MCQ 17. In IVF, when is embryo transfer usually done? Usually at day 3, when embryo is at 6–8 cell stage. MCQ 18. Ovulation is diagnosed by all, EXCEPT: Mittelschmerz pain, slight vaginal bleeding, rise in basal body temperature, stretchable cervical mucus, rise in serum progesterone on day 21, secretory endometrium—all are signs. But measuring serum progesterone on day 14 is not useful. So answer is: serum progesterone on day 14. MCQ 19. Independent assortment of paternal and maternal chromosomes occurs in which stage? It occurs during meiosis I (primary → secondary spermatocyte). MCQ 20. Velocity of sperm? About 1–4 mm per minute. (Approx 3 mm/min given.) MCQ 21. What is “superfecundation”? It means fertilization of two or more ova by sperms from separate acts of intercourse. If by same intercourse → twins; if by separate acts, possibly involving even different fathers, it’s superfecundation. MCQ 22. A woman gives birth to twins, but DNA reveals only one belongs to father—this condition is: “superfecundation.” MCQ 23. Glycoproteins of zona pellucida include: ZP1, ZP2, ZP3. So the answer option containing all three (ZP1, 2, 3) is correct. MCQ 24. Development of an egg without fertilization is called: Parthenogenesis. MCQ 25. Site of fertilization in human: Ampullary region of fallopian tube. MCQ 26. What is cortical reaction? Upon sperm entry, cortical granules in egg release contents, causing a calcium wave and modification of ovum membrane, forming fertilization membrane, which blocks polyspermy. So the correct answer is: release of cortical granules → block polyspermy. MCQ 27. Acrosomal reaction? Acrosome releases enzymes (hyaluronidase, acrosin) which digest corona radiata and zona pellucida, allowing sperm to contact egg membrane. Correct answer = digestion of zona pellucida, permitting sperm contact. MCQ 28. Clinical scenario: A truck driver with long hours near engine heat, infertility of five years. Female partner normal cycles, no problems. Most likely cause: exposure to prolonged heat in scrotal region impairing spermatogenesis. So, students, these are the MCQs on fertilization. I’ll see you across the screen in another lecture.

Both things together will make you better prepared next time. Let’s begin with spinal cord MCQs part 3. This time we are going to deal with MCQs on ascending tracts as well as blood supply of the spinal cord. Which ascending tracts? Basically, lateral spinothalamic tract, dorsal columns, and so on. Let’s begin with the first MCQ. MCQ 1: “Following is true for lateral spinothalamic tract (EXCEPT).” Remember, this is an “except” type—so three options will be correct, and one wrong. The lateral spinothalamic tract is the tract carrying pain and temperature. The first-order neuron lies in the ipsilateral dorsal root ganglion. The second-order neuron lies in the contralateral posterior grey horn. These fibers cross over almost at the same level at which sensation enters into the spinal cord, and then ascend as lateral spinothalamic tract to the contralateral thalamus. From there, third-order neurons in the contralateral thalamus relay sensation to contralateral cerebral cortex (sensory area). So pain on one side is perceived in the cerebral cortex of the opposite side. Now back to the MCQ: 1st order neuron—ipsilateral dorsal root ganglion → correct. 2nd order neuron—posterior grey horn → correct. 3rd order neuron—NO, not in lower medulla. It is in contralateral thalamus. Final relay—contralateral sensory part of cerebral cortex → correct. So option C (third order neuron in lower medulla) is the wrong one. That is your answer. Another important point: lesion of lateral spinothalamic tract produces contralateral loss of pain and temperature. So the correct MCQ answer is: contralateral loss of pain & temperature occurs in injury to lateral spinothalamic tract. MCQ 2: “Lateral spinothalamic tract carries which sensation?” Options given: pain from contralateral side—correct. Pain from ipsilateral side—no. Pressure sensations—no. So the correct answer is: pain from contralateral side of the body. MCQ 3: “Following is true for lateral spinothalamic tract, except.” 1st order neuron in dorsal root ganglion—yes. 2nd order neuron in posterior grey horn—yes. Collateral to reticular activating system—yes. 3rd order neuron in ipsilateral thalamus—no. It’s in contralateral thalamus. So answer is D. That’s how you analyze systematically. MCQ 4: “Which lemniscus carries pain sensation?” Now think: lemnisci in the midbrain include medial, trigeminal, spinal lemniscus, and lateral lemniscus. Medial—fine touch. Trigeminal—proprioception for head/neck. Spinal lemniscus—pain & temperature. Lateral lemniscus—hearing. So answer = spinal lemniscus. MCQ 5: “Which of these tracts are ascending EXCEPT?” Options include pyramidal, fasciculus gracilis, fasciculus cuneatus, spinotectal. Answer is pyramidal tracts—they are descending, not ascending. MCQ 6: “First order neuron in all ascending tracts is where?” Answer—always dorsal root ganglion. Right. MCQ 7: “Internal arcuate fibers are—?” Internal arcuate fibers are sensory fibers crossing in medulla to form medial lemniscus. Posterior external arcuates → sensory fibers entering cerebellum. Anterior external arcuates → descending fibers across anterior medulla. Internal arcuates → sensory decussation in medulla. Answer: sensory fibers crossing to form medial lemniscus. MCQ 8: “Longest neuron of the body?” Options: pyramidal cell of cerebral cortex, anterior horn cell neuron, dorsal root ganglion cell carrying sensation from great toe, retinal ganglion cell. The longest is dorsal root ganglion cell carrying sensation from great toe → travels whole length of body up to medulla. Answer is dorsal root ganglion cell of great toe. MCQ 9: “Lesion of dorsal column produces what?” Options: astereognosis, loss of vibration, ataxia, complete loss of touch. Dorsal column lesion produces loss of vibration sense, astereognosis, and ataxia. But not complete loss of touch—because anterior spinothalamic tract partially carries crude touch. So the answer is not complete loss of touch. MCQ 10: From here we discussed method of “blocks of memory”—for each tract/lesion, make 1 block and keep it. Lesion of dorsal column produces ipsilateral: loss of tactile localisation, loss of vibration, loss of proprioception, astereognosis—but NOT loss of pain. Pain is carried by spinothalamic. MCQ 11: Which names are of spinocerebellar tracts except? Answer: there is no lateral spinocerebellar tract. You have anterior, posterior, cuneocerebellar—but no lateral. MCQ 12: About spinocerebellar tracts, except? Posterior spinocerebellar—fibers from Clarke’s column, uncrossed. Anterior spinocerebellar—cross, then recross, finally enter superior cerebellar peduncle. Fibers of spinocerebellar go via superior peduncle, yes. Cuneocerebellar fibers are posterior external arcuates, not anterior. Answer: incorrect statement is “cuneocerebellar fibers = anterior external arcuates.” MCQ 13: “Which nucleus is crucial relay in spinocerebellar tract?” Answer: Clarke’s column. MCQ 14: “Blood supply of spinal cord?” Two main arteries: anterior spinal artery & posterior spinal arteries—both branches of vertebral artery. Additional segmental arteries strengthen with radicular branches. Sources include deep cervical, ascending cervical, intercostals, lumbar arteries. Anterior spinal artery supplies anterior two-thirds of cord. Posterior spinal arteries supply posterior one-third. MCQ 15: “Arteria radicularis magna (of Adamkiewicz): following are true except?” It is also called arteria of Adamkiewicz, branch of aorta, usually arises from left side, supplies lower two-thirds of spinal cord. Wrong is: “arises from upper thoracic.” Actually, it arises from lower thoracic or upper lumbar, usually left. Answer: incorrect → arises from upper thoracic. MCQ 16: “Two vertebral arteries unite to form?” Common sense—basilar artery. MCQ 17: Blood supply true except? Posterior spinal artery—supplies posterior one-third → true. Venous plexus communicates with surrounding venous sinuses → true. Arteria of Adamkiewicz origin from upper thoracic vertebra → false. Single anterior spinal artery formed from both vertebrals → true. So incorrect statement is: origin is upper thoracic. So that covers ascending tract and blood supply MCQs.
