Hello. How do we really understand the medulla? The medulla appears like a whitish nervous tissue, very difficult at first to appreciate. Each structure within it—the nuclei, tracts, fibers—is so intricate that unless it is broken down into sectional slices, it becomes confusing. What anatomists did: they took the medulla, sliced it section by section, stained, and carefully delineated the structures with functions. And finally it was decided that for undergraduate understanding, one should study the medulla at three key levels: Lowermost section – through the pyramidal decussation. Middle section – at the level of sensory relay nuclei. Upper, open medulla section – at the level of the hypoglossal and dorsal vagal nuclei, etc. Today we are studying only the first level: the lowermost medulla, at the level of pyramidal decussation.

Stepwise Drawing and Orientation 
As always, I ask you to sit down with a drawing book or digital tablet, and develop the section along with me. Believe me, it is the best way. Imagine a transverse section through medulla at its beginning. It looks like spinal cord: central canal in the middle, gray matter around it, white matter outside, posterior and anterior median fissures. So basically, the medulla’s lowermost section starts off looking like a modified spinal cord. But as you move upward, the anterior region bulges forward. These swellings are the pyramids. Draw them on both sides in the anterior part of medulla. Color them: these represent bundles of longitudinal descending fibers.

The Pyramids 
Pyramids are formed by descending motor fibers: 
Corticospinal fibers 
Corticobulbar fibers 
Corticopontine fibers 
These originate in the cerebral cortex, pass through midbrain and pons, and collect anteriorly in the medulla forming the swellings called pyramids. 
Corticospinal fibers: descend to spinal cord to control voluntary movements of limbs and trunk. 
Corticobulbar fibers: terminate in cranial nerve motor nuclei in brainstem to control muscles of head/neck. 
Corticopontine fibers: terminate in pontine nuclei and then relay to cerebellum to help in coordination/balance. 
So pyramids are conglomerates of these three fiber-sets.

Great Motor Decussation 
Now, the key event at this level: the decussation of corticospinal fibers. About 70–90% of the corticospinal fibers cross midline here in the medulla, forming the lateral corticospinal tract of the opposite side. The rest remain uncrossed and descend as the anterior corticospinal tract. This decussation is called the Great Motor Decussation. Its significance: Because of this crossing, the left cerebral cortex controls motor activity on the right half of the body, and vice versa. So remember: Lesion above decussation → symptoms appear on the contralateral body. Lesion below decussation → symptoms on the ipsilateral side.

Effect on Gray Matter 
As fibers cross through the central gray matter, they actually break and divide portions of it. The bit of gray matter split off forms the supraspinal nucleus. This nucleus becomes the origin point for: 
Ventral root of C1 spinal nerve, and 
Cranial rootlets of the spinal accessory nerve. 
So from the decussation, you have both the crucial corticospinal crossing event and emergence of accessory-related rootlets.

Posterior Gray and White Matter 
Now turn posteriorly. In the posterior gray column and its overlying white cap you see: 
Spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve, 
Spinal tract of trigeminal nerve. 
These extend caudally into the medulla. Together, they form the seat where pain and temperature sensations from the face are processed.

Pain & Temperature Pathway from Face 
Trigeminal nerve is the chief sensory nerve of the face. It has three sensory nuclei: 
Mesencephalic – proprioception 
Principal sensory – touch/pressure 
Spinal nucleus – pain and temperature 
So: pain/temperature from the face travels: 
Face receptors → trigeminal nerve → trigeminal ganglion → spinal tract of trigeminal → spinal trigeminal nucleus. 
Here, fibers cross to opposite side and ascend as the ventral trigeminothalamic tract, going to the thalamus, then to cerebral cortex, where they are recognized as pain/temperature in face. 
This is exactly analogous to body pain/temperature carried by lateral spinothalamic tract, except here it’s for face.

Dorsal Column Nuclei 
The posterior gray columns also show two swellings: 
Nucleus gracilis, 
Nucleus cuneatus. 
These are the relay stations of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway. 
Fibers here will decussate later as internal arcuate fibers and form medial lemniscus.

Add Ascending and Descending Tracts 
In our medullary section, also draw: 
Ascending: lateral spinothalamic, anterior spinothalamic, spinocerebellar tracts. 
Descending: rubrospinal tract, corticospinal, olivospinal, vestibulospinal—all running here. 
Remember, medulla acts as a highway: ascending fibers from spinal cord to brain, and descending fibers from cortex to spinal cord, they must traverse this region.

Quick Revision 
So at the level of Great Motor Decussation we have: 
Anterior pyramids = corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine fibers. 
Great motor decussation = 70–90% corticospinal fibers crossing → lateral corticospinal tracts. 
Remaining → anterior corticospinal tracts. 
Supraspinal nucleus derived from disrupted gray, giving C1 ventral root, accessory nerve rootlets. 
Spinal nucleus and tract of trigeminal = pain/temperature face. 
Dorsal column nuclei = fine touch, vibration from body. 
Multiple ascending/descending tracts passing through.

Clinical Significance 
Because of pyramidal decussation: cortical lesions produce contralateral motor deficit, spinal cord lesions produce ipsilateral motor deficit. 
Because of spinal nucleus of trigeminal here: facial pain/temperature are relayed → lesion can cause ipsilateral facial analgesia with contralateral body analgesia.

So today we studied the lowermost medulla at the level of pyramidal decussation. We saw: 
The pyramids, 
Crossing call the great motor decussation, 
Supraspinal nucleus origins, 
Spinal trigeminal tract & nucleus, 
Nuclei gracilis and cuneatus, 
Ascending/descending tract profile. 
Practice the diagram carefully – because often in exam you are asked: “Draw and label a section of medulla at level of pyramidal decussation.” 
Along with labels, you must explain the significance. 
In the next lecture, we will go to the middle medulla level. 
Take a break, revise this once, internalize the drawing. 
We will see you in the next lecture on medulla oblongata.

Hello my dear students. Today’s lecture is about the Surgical Anatomy of Piles (Hemorrhoids and Hemorrhoidectomy). In first-year MBBS, students often encounter the term “piles” or “hemorrhoidectomy,” but to understand it properly, you need to revise the surgical anatomy of the rectum and anal canal. 

Brief Anatomy of Rectum and Anal Canal 
Here is the rectum and the anal canal. The rectum passes through the levator ani (pelvic diaphragm). This divides it into upper rectum and lower anal canal. Laterally, it is supported by the pararectal fascia. We further subdivide the anal canal using the pectinate (dentate) line and Hilton’s line into upper, middle, and lower parts. The wall of the anal canal has the internal anal sphincter (thickened inner circular muscle) and the external anal sphincter (made up of deep, superficial, and subcutaneous parts). Running longitudinally is an outer muscle coat forming a fibroelastic conjoint sheath, joining at Hilton’s line, creating the anal intermuscular septum. This is the basic anatomy.

Venous drainage and venous plexuses 
Between the sphincters and within the anal canal wall are venous plexuses: Internal venous plexus above (within anal columns, above pectinate line). External venous plexus below (under skin around anus). They communicate with each other across the anal intermuscular septum. Now: The internal venous plexus drains into the superior rectal vein, which continues upward and opens into the inferior mesenteric vein → portal circulation. Thus, blood from above the pectinate line is drained to the portal system. The middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac vein → systemic (caval) circulation. Therefore, the anal venous plexus is a site of porto-systemic anastomosis. Portal system = superior rectal vein. Systemic system = middle and inferior rectal veins.

Hemorrhoids (Piles) 
When these venous plexuses become swollen and varicose → they form hemorrhoids (piles). Internal piles: Originate above pectinate line, covered by mucous membrane. Painless, because nerve supply is autonomic. They prolapse downward but usually don’t cause pain. External piles: Originate below pectinate line, covered by skin. Painful, because supplied by inferior rectal nerves (somatic). They form tender, painful lumps near anal margin. So the key difference: Internal piles above dentate line – mucosa-covered, painless, may prolapse. External piles below dentate line – skin-covered, painful, do not prolapse.

Anal Cushions 
Remember also the concept of anal cushions: These are normal submucosal structures in the anal canal, containing blood vessels, connective tissue, and smooth muscle. They bulge inward, helping maintain continence by creating a “seal” for the anal canal. However, sometimes these cushions degenerate → veins inside them dilate and become varicose → these are what we recognize as primary hemorrhoids.

Position of Primary Piles 
If you look at the patient in lithotomy position (from below), typical primary piles occur at three constant sites: Left lateral, Right anterior, Right posterior.

Why do Piles occur? 
Absence of valves in rectal venous system. Veins must drain against gravity. Compression of veins as they pierce rectal wall. Raised portal venous pressure (portal hypertension). Chronic straining (constipation, pregnancy). All these predispose veins to dilatation and varicosity.

Clinical & Surgical Importance 
Because internal hemorrhoids are painless (autonomic supply), surgery can be done under minimal anesthesia, sometimes even in an outpatient setting. External hemorrhoids are painful (rich somatic nerve supply), so anesthesia and careful peri-operative management are essential in hemorrhoidectomy. Nerve supply differences thus dictate surgical planning and patient comfort.

Summary 
Today we learned: Anatomy of rectum and anal canal. Internal vs external venous plexuses. Superior rectal vein (portal) vs middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic) → site of porto-systemic anastomosis. Internal vs external hemorrhoids: coverings, nerve supply, pain, prolapse. Anal cushions: their role in continence, and how degeneration → primary piles. Sites of primary piles: left lateral, right anterior, right posterior. Clinical implication of nerve supply in surgery.

Hello my dear students. This lecture is part of my Central Nervous System series, titled The Anatomy of the Spinal Cord: Extrapyramidal System. We are often a little unsure about what exactly this so-called extrapyramidal system or extrapyramidal tracts are. So today, I want to take you through the topic in a very short but precise way—just the essentials. You don’t need to go into too many details, but you must know: What are the extrapyramidal tracts, What does each do, How they function in relation to pyramidal tracts. Links for all the other spinal cord lectures are given in the description, and they are also available on the website. Currently, they are free to access on YouTube, but after two months they will be accessible for a small fee from the website. Alright, let’s begin. 

Quick Recap – Ascending vs Descending Tracts 
Your body generates sensory stimulation: pain, touch, vibration, proprioception. All of these sensory inputs travel upward through ascending tracts, e.g.: 
Lateral spinothalamic tract: pain and temperature. 
Anterior spinothalamic tract: crude touch and pressure. 
Dorsal column tracts (gracilis + cuneatus): fine touch, vibration, two-point discrimination, proprioception. 
Trigeminal lemniscus: sensory input from head and face. 
Lateral lemniscus: auditory sensations. 
Spinotectal tract: reflex coordination of head/eye to body movements. 
Spinocerebellar tracts (anterior and posterior): unconscious proprioception for balance. 
So the brain becomes aware through ascending tracts. The question is: what does the brain do with this information? It analyzes it and sends commands downwards through descending tracts. 

Descending Tracts 
From cerebral cortex: 
Lateral corticospinal tract 
Anterior corticospinal tract 
(These are pyramidal tracts since they originate directly from the cortex.) 
From brainstem structures (not directly cortex): 
Rubrospinal tract: from red nucleus of midbrain. 
Tectospinal tract: from superior colliculus. 
Vestibulospinal tract: from vestibular nuclei in pons/medulla. 
Reticulospinal tracts: from reticular formation. 
Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF): from vestibular nuclei, interconnecting cranial nerve nuclei. 
So here is the key point: Tracts from cortex = pyramidal. Tracts from anywhere else (brainstem) = extrapyramidal. That’s what we are studying today. 

1. Rubrospinal Tract 
Origin: Red nucleus in midbrain (at the level of superior colliculus). 
Red nucleus receives input from cerebral cortex, cerebellum, thalamus, globus pallidus. 
It integrates this and sends descending fibers. 
Pathway: Fibers cross immediately (ventral tegmental decussation of Forel) and descend in front of the lateral corticospinal tract in the spinal cord. 
Action: Facilitatory to flexors, inhibitory to extensors. 
That’s the one sentence you must remember about rubrospinal tract. 
Alternative pathway to pyramidal system. 

2. Tectospinal Tract 
Origin: Superior colliculus (seat of visual reflexes). 
Superior colliculus receives inputs from retina, visual cortex, spinal cord, and inferior colliculus (auditory). 
Fibers cross dorsally (dorsal tegmental decussation) and descend as the tectospinal tract. 
Action: Coordinates audio-visual reflexes. 
For example, in a dark room, a sudden flash of light or a loud horn makes you automatically turn your eyes and head toward it. 
This tract mainly influences the upper cervical cord to turn head and eyes—it does not descend below thoracic segments. 

3. Vestibulospinal Tract 
Origin: Vestibular nuclei in pons/medulla. 
They receive input from vestibular nerve (inner ear), cerebellum, and other areas. 
Fibers descend mainly as lateral vestibulospinal tract (long descending). 
Some ascend/descend briefly as medial vestibulospinal tract in the brainstem/cervical cord. 
Action: Maintains posture and equilibrium. 
It is facilitatory to extensors, inhibitory to flexors. 
So whenever you stand upright, your extensors hold you steady thanks to vestibulospinal action. 

4. Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) 
Origin: vestibular nuclei → cross midline → ascend and descend in brainstem/cervical cord. 
Action: Coordinates eye movements with head and neck movements. 
It interconnects cranial nerve nuclei (III, IV, VI, XI) with vestibular input. 
Example: conjugate gaze movements (eyes move together when head turns). 

5. Reticulospinal Tract 
Origin: Reticular formation. 
Fibers descend bilaterally. 
Action: Important for muscle tone maintenance, especially antigravity muscles. 
Facilitatory to extensors, inhibitory to flexors. 
Particularly essential for upright posture. 

Cerebellar Influence 
Remember: cerebellum is constantly monitoring. 
It receives unconscious proprioception via spinocerebellar tracts, analyzes it, and then sends output through red nucleus, vestibular nuclei, and reticular formation. 
This means cerebellum modulates rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal tracts → ensuring smooth movement and body balance. 

Summary of Actions 
Rubrospinal: Facilitates flexors, inhibits extensors. 
Tectospinal: Audio-visual reflex movements of head/neck. 
Vestibulospinal: Facilitates extensors, inhibits flexors → balance. 
Medial longitudinal fasciculus: Coordination of eye and head. 
Reticulospinal: Maintains posture, tone of antigravity muscles. 

So students, today we discussed the Extrapyramidal tracts in brief. Too many details would get confusing; this short structured form is what you need to remember. Revise it once or twice—you’ll be comfortable recalling them. Spinal cord anatomy is the strong foundation required for CNS, so do not skip it. If you missed any earlier lecture, watch it here. We are all the time talking about portal vein—portal vein supplies blood to the liver, veins drain into portal vein, porto-caval anastomosis, portal hypertension—I think it’s time we studied the anatomy of portal vein and its surgical anatomy. So today, the topic is Surgical Anatomy of Portal Vein. 

So, what is the portal vein? The portal vein is a vein that drains blood from your gut—simple. Except for the lower part of the anal canal which is not drained by portal vein. It also drains blood from spleen, pancreas, and gall bladder. So here is the concept map of the portal vein: from the GIT (except lower end of anal canal), from the spleen, pancreas, gall bladder—blood drains into the portal vein. This portal vein carries all this nutrient-loaded blood into the liver and branches out into right and left branches, releasing the blood into the liver through sinusoids. The blood now flows through sinusoids, then finally drains into hepatic veins—right, middle and left—and drains into the inferior vena cava. So this is what the portal vein is all about, from where of course the blood flows into systemic circulation. This in short is your portal vein. 

It has some peculiarities—it’s not like any other. It’s a little unique vein in that it begins in capillaries and ends in capillaries. Did you note that? It begins in the form of capillaries from the gut, forms a proper vein, and then again breaks up into capillaries in the liver. Normally, veins are formed and drain blood, they don’t break back again, isn’t it? So that makes portal vein rather unique. Also, it’s got no valves. It acts as a massive reservoir of blood—almost it is said that 1/4 to 1/3 of your total blood can stay in the portal vein. It conveys blood products which are absorbed from the gut into the liver. And it’s got two streams of blood flowing through—one coming from superior mesenteric vein which is carrying blood loaded with absorbed products from gut, the other is coming from the spleen, which is carrying products like breakdown products for RBCs and so on. Finally, it provides 66–75% of the blood requirement of liver. That’s your portal vein. 

Let’s learn a little bit more about it. It is formed by union of superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein, behind the neck of pancreas, in front of inferior vena cava. Wait—you will understand it. Here is the formation, behind the neck of pancreas. It just has two parts to it: an extra-hepatic part (which lies outside the liver), and an intra-hepatic part (which lies within the liver). The extra-hepatic part, as you can see, is divided by the duodenum into: infra-duodenal, retro-duodenal and supra-duodenal parts. I hope you are understanding all this. And then of course, the rest of the portal vein divides and branches off into the liver. That’s the outline. 

So—infra-duodenal part: which is below the duodenum. It is related posteriorly to the inferior vena cava, on the right to the bile duct, in front to the neck of pancreas. As it rises upwards, it slowly slides behind the duodenum here. Okay. Here it is anteriorly related to the first part of duodenum. On the right it is related to the common bile duct. Now it slides further upwards to pass above the duodenum: this is the supra-duodenal part. As you can see, this part is enclosed within the two folds of lesser omentum in the right free margin of lesser omentum, such that—on the left and anterior it is related to the hepatic artery proper, on the right anterior it is related to the bile duct. 

This portal vein now reaches the porta hepatis, where you can see it dividing into right and left branches. At the porta hepatis it is related anteriorly to the two hepatic ducts, and to the two hepatic arteries—right and left. Structures at porta hepatis, remember the mnemonic “DAV”—Duct, Artery, Vein: hepatic ducts (D), hepatic artery (A), and portal vein (V). Also present here is the hepatic plexus of nerves, cystic duct, lymphatics from the liver. So that’s the set. 

Now see the splenic vein—splenic vein also receives inferior mesenteric vein. The portal vein, as it ascends upwards toward the liver, receives: superior pancreaticoduodenal vein, left gastric vein (which also receives oesophageal veins), right gastric vein (which may receive prepyloric vein). All this blood now reaches the porta hepatis, and the portal vein divides into right and left branches. The right branch also receives the cystic vein. The left branch receives the paraumbilical veins, which are present in the free margin of falciform ligament. 

Now we go to the intra-hepatic part—what does the portal vein do inside the liver? Inside the liver, remember, the portal vein releases blood into portal canals in the form of branches. From portal canal, blood goes into hepatic sinusoids, then into central veins, then into hepatic veins, and finally into inferior vena cava. That’s it. Also, within the liver, remember the portal vein divides almost at a level such that it helps to divide your liver into superior and inferior half—which is very important regarding the Couinaud’s segments. There is a separate lecture on Couinaud’s segments of liver: please go and see that to understand further details. 

But here, now you can see your portal vein dividing into right branch of portal vein and the left branch of portal vein. The right branch now divides into: two anterior branches (anterior superior, anterior inferior), two posterior branches (postero-superior, postero-inferior). The left branch divides into: lateral and medial—lateral superior, lateral inferior, medial superior, medial inferior. And both the branches supply the caudate lobe. Got it? So the level at which your portal vein branches out helps to divide your liver into upper half (superior half) and inferior half. Please access the Couinaud segments of liver lecture to understand those eight segments and their anatomy. 

So, let’s talk about the surgical anatomy of portal vein—which is very important. Just take a pause, breathe in, and let’s go into the surgical anatomy. Portal vein has a central role to play in the venous drainage of gastrointestinal tract. So understanding its anatomy is crucial for almost all surgical procedures involving abdomen—so involving liver, involving pancreas, involving other parts of the GIT. In liver surgeries—in hepatic surgeries such as liver resection—you have to know and have a precise knowledge of portal vein anatomy, so that you don’t end up having a massive bleed in surgery. 

In conditions like portal hypertension, in case of cirrhosis of liver, you have so many varices happening and ascites happening—you have to know the anatomy of portal vein to understand and treat these conditions. Surgical interventions like porto-systemic shunts of liver may be required to be made—in which case, you have to know the anatomy of portal vein. Take a look at this image—you are seeing the portal vein branching out, you are seeing the hepatic veins, and you are seeing a porto-systemic shunt, shunting blood from the portal vein into the hepatic vein, bypassing the liver. This is treatment of porto-caval anastomosis related complications—important treatment. You must understand this. 

So—that’s another lecture created. Access that to understand more. For pancreas surgery also, because of the close proximity of the portal vein, you have to know the anatomy well. Otherwise, it can lead to severe hemorrhage. In case of tumor also, portal vein, which is so centrally situated, can lead to life-threatening complications. Portal vein has got its own set of anatomical variations. Before operating on any planned abdominal surgery, pre-operative imaging and planning should be done so that such variations are identified. Thus, the portal vein anatomy and its relationship with surrounding structures is crucial for surgical practice. Mastery of portal vein helps in prevention of intra-operative complications, successful execution of complex surgeries.
